claims.claim: A table in a relational database consists of rows and columns; the number and order of the columns is fixed, each column has a name, and the number of rows is variable, reflecting how much data is stored at a given moment.
A column is a vertical entity in a table, while a record, also called a row, is each individual entry in the table and is a horizontal entity.
An attribute is a distinctive feature, characteristic, or property of an object; in a table, each column holds one such property, with one value recorded for every row.
The words column, field, and attribute are used for the same structure: a vertical set of values for one property, with 'field' coming from file-based data systems and 'attribute' from data modeling.
Every column has a name and a declared type; database systems provide type families such as numeric, character (text), and date/time.
A not-null (must-be-filled) constraint requires a column to have a value in every row; by default, a column may hold no value.
A unique constraint ensures that all values in a column are different from one another; no two rows may share the same value in that column.

The declared set of columns gives a table its structure and meaning: without column definitions, a collection of values cannot be interpreted, because nothing says what each value is or what it belongs to.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Column vs field vs attribute: are the three terms strictly synonymous?
positions: Everyday tutorials such as W3Schools use column and field interchangeably for the same structure (a NOT NULL rule is described as enforcing a field to always contain a value).
Formal relational-model and data-modeling texts reserve 'attribute' as the theoretical term for a column, and 'field' carries an older, file-based connotation.
The NIST glossary defines attribute generally as a property of an object, not specifically as a database column.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: At this literacy level the lesson treats column, field, and attribute as three names for the same idea, notes their different origins (SQL, file-based systems, data modeling), and does not claim strict formal equivalence beyond what the tutorials support.

sourceRecords.title: NIST Glossary: attribute
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Defines an attribute as 'any distinctive feature, characteristic, or property of an object'. Used as the Tier A anchor for the attribute-as-property meaning behind column terminology; no prose adapted.

sourceRecords.title: PostgreSQL 18 Documentation: 5.1. Table Basics
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. States that a relational table consists of rows and columns, that the number and order of columns is fixed, that each column has a name, and that the number of rows is variable. Supports the fixed-columns/variable-rows claim and the named-column claim.

sourceRecords.title: PostgreSQL 18 Documentation: 5.5. Constraints
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Introduces constraints as a way to restrict data beyond what types allow and covers not-null and unique constraints. Supports the constraint concept at intuition level; no SQL shown in the lesson.

sourceRecords.title: PostgreSQL 18 Documentation: Chapter 8. Data Types
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Chapter organizes types into numeric, character, and date/time families. Supports the claim that a column's type is chosen from families such as numbers, text, and dates. Reference-level only; the data-types sibling topic owns depth.

sourceRecords.title: SQLite Documentation: CREATE TABLE
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. Describes each column of a table as having a name, a declared type, and optional constraints, and lists UNIQUE and NOT NULL among supported constraints. Supports the column name/type/constraint structure claim.

sourceRecords.title: W3Schools: SQL Introduction
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. States that a column is a vertical entity in a table and a record (row) is a horizontal entity; example columns (CustomerID, CustomerName, Address, City, Country) support the naming intuition. Facts synthesized into original prose.

sourceRecords.title: W3Schools: SQL NOT NULL Constraint
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. States that the NOT NULL constraint enforces a column to not accept NULL values, that this enforces a field to always contain a value, and that by default a column can hold NULL values. Supports the must-be-filled rule and the field/column synonym.

sourceRecords.title: W3Schools: SQL UNIQUE Constraint
sourceRecords.notes: Read live 2026-08-21. States that the UNIQUE constraint ensures that all values in a column are unique. Supports the must-be-unique rule at intuition level.
